source.title: Unlocking Latent Value: Taxonomy-Guided Recovery of High-Performing Data from Low-Tier Web Corpora
source.authors: Neeraj Varshney; Sanket Lokegaonkar; Nasser Zalmout; Qing-Yu Yin; Priyanka Nigam; Bing Yin

record.tranche_reason: The study compares small-scale screening results with a larger compute ladder to test whether screening predicts relative performance, but it does not fit or reproduce the original power-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The study reports many results comparing taxonomy-filtered and unfiltered datasets at L10. Those filtering comparisons are not recorded as rows unless they bear on prediction across compute. The paper reports that the L10 ordering persists across the full ladder and gives several L12 benchmark losses. The plotted curves do not provide extractable numeric values at the other rungs.
record.test_reason: This is a data-filtering study. It uses a scaling-law compute ladder (L4–L12, 13.8B–56.6B tokens, about 4x) as an evaluation tool and reports only how its filters perform against unfiltered baselines. It fits no power law and extrapolates no fitted curve to larger runs. Its one cross-scale claim, that the L10 filter ordering holds up to L12, covers about 1.3x in tokens and concerns data-recipe ranking, not loss prediction. The answer-loss-vs-FLOPs curves are plotted only, never fitted or quantified as a scaling trend, so none of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors' main conclusion is that multi-dimensional taxonomy filtering, timeliness especially, recovers latent value from deprioritized web tiers. Filtered mid-tier and lower-tier data beats unfiltered top-tier data on reasoning and coding, at a small knowledge-breadth cost on MMLU. They treat 'L10 is a reliable proxy' as validation of their screening method, asserted from qualitative ordering in Figure 4.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a compute ladder and L10 screening to evaluate data-filter configurations; it does not fit the original power-law loss curves or optimize parameter-token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Benchmark and filter choice affect outcomes: the selected filter performs especially well on reasoning and coding, while MMLU reflects a knowledge-breadth tradeoff. The paper also reports results for distinct data tiers.

fits_no_version.finding: The ranking of data-filter configurations at the L10 screening scale (42.8B tokens) is reported as preserved across the L4–L12 ladder. No rank statistic is given, and only F8 and the baselines were run on the ladder.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relative rankings of pretraining data recipes measured at small scale persist at larger compute scales.

fits_no_version.finding: At L12, F8-filtered mid-tier data has lower benchmark answer loss than unfiltered bucket 200 on GSM8K, Minerva-Math, HumanEval and MBPP, but not on MMLU.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Data composition shifts benchmark answer-loss curves across a compute ladder, with a capability-specific tradeoff.

record.problems: The corpus is proprietary. The full ladder validates a selected filter rather than the whole candidate space. Numeric results for most ladder rungs are available only in plots, and the text reports no uncertainty estimates for the ladder outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Pass 1 and Pass 2 filtering results are omitted because they compare data-filter configurations at L10 rather than test power-law scaling or prediction across compute. Lower-tier L12 filtering outcomes are also omitted for the same reason.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Curves are plotted on log-log axes over about 1.75 decades of FLOPs but not fitted.
No fitted law is extrapolated. Ladder results are reported only as qualitative ordering, over about 1.3x tokens beyond the screening scale.
No allocation of parameters versus tokens at fixed compute.
No other modalities or training regimes are fitted to power laws.
No quantified relation between benchmark loss and scale or pretraining loss. Benchmark answer loss against FLOPs appears only in figures, with no fit or numbers.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices. The dependence of curves on the data filter is shown but no exponents are fitted.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/tests classification was wrong. Scaling-law ladders are used only as an evaluation tool, citing Hoffmann et al. as the source of ladder methodology. There are no power-law fits, exponents or extrapolated predictions, and the ladder spans only 13.8B to 56.6B tokens. All rows are relinked to none and no verdicts are given. The proprietary corpus and the lack of uncertainty estimates further limit use.

versions.untested_parts: The paper plots answer loss against compute, but does not report a power-law fit or establish that held-out pretraining loss follows a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Tests whether L10 screening preserves relative filter ordering on the full ladder; does not report small-run-fitted power laws or predicted numerical losses for much larger runs.
Does not optimize parameter and token allocation at fixed compute.
Does not compare architecture depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Does not test whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests preservation of relative benchmark-loss ordering across compute for the selected filtering comparison; does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices or setups, or test whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: L4–L12 training runs
rows.operation_detail: Compared L10 screening results with full scaling-law ladder results for selected filter configurations.
rows.measure: Consistency of relative performance ordering between L10 screening and the full compute ladder
rows.value: The paper states that the ordering observed at L10 is preserved across the full compute range.
rows.note: This is a reported consistency of ordering, not a report of small-run-fitted power laws or predicted numerical losses.
rows.check: Preserved rank of filters from L10 (42.8B tokens) to L12 (56.6B) is a claim about the screening proxy. It is not small-run power-law fits predicting much larger runs (V2), and it is not downstream predictability from scale or loss (V6). It is stated qualitatively, with no rank correlation or numbers. Belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: L4–L12 training runs
rows.operation_detail: Measured GSM8K answer loss across the compute ladder for F8-filtered and unfiltered data.
rows.measure: Benchmark answer loss; relative ordering across compute
rows.value: At L12, F8 loss 103.9; reported as 6.2% below unfiltered buckets 191–199 and 2.5% below bucket 200. The paper states that the L10 ordering persists across the ladder.
rows.note: The numeric L12 value is stated in text; other rung values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: Compares F8-filtered with unfiltered data at L12 on GSM8K answer loss. This is the study's own method against baselines, not how downstream performance scales. Not V6.

rows.subject: L4–L12 training runs
rows.operation_detail: Measured Minerva-Math answer loss across the compute ladder for F8-filtered and unfiltered data.
rows.measure: Benchmark answer loss; relative ordering across compute
rows.value: At L12, F8 loss 235.7; reported as an 18.0% improvement over unfiltered buckets 191–199 and a 10.9% improvement over bucket 200. The paper states that the L10 ordering persists across the ladder.
rows.note: The numeric L12 value is stated in text; other rung values are shown only in the figure.
rows.check: Filter-versus-baseline comparison at L12 (Minerva-Math). This is the study's own method's performance, not a scaling result.

rows.subject: L4–L12 training runs
rows.operation_detail: Measured MMLU answer loss across the compute ladder for F8-filtered and unfiltered data.
rows.measure: Benchmark answer loss; relative ordering across compute
rows.value: At L12, F8 loss 16.82. It improves over unfiltered buckets 191–199 but is higher than unfiltered bucket 200. The paper states that the L10 ordering persists across the ladder.
rows.note: The result preserves a relative ordering across compute but does not make F8 the best of the stated comparisons on MMLU.
rows.check: Filter-versus-baseline comparison at L12 (MMLU, 16.82 vs 17.17 and 16.20). The 'partial' state refers to F8 not beating bucket 200, which says nothing about any scaling-law version.
